title: Introduction to idmapper
text: Say help run community running club, want join together three datasets describe runners, extracted different systems don’t share common key: race_results - race-timing company ran last month’s 10k. One row per runner, identified whatever email used registering race. fitness_app_leaderboard - GPS running app members use track training. One row per runner, identified app username, whatever email signed app - sometimes email registered race , sometimes different one entirely. club_roster - club’s membership system. One row per member, listing member ID, app username, race-registration email, app-signup email together. None data real - ’s entirely synthetic, invented example. Notice Sam Okafor: race_results email registered race , fitness_app_leaderboard different email entirely - one happened sign running app years earlier. two rows share identifier directly - place connects club_roster, happens list emails side side. plain join email simply miss : Sam’s total_distance_km comes back NA - doesn’t use app (’s logged 298 km ), join way know sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com samokafor.trains@fastmail.com person. patch one case hand, doesn’t scale, won’t always human around notice mismatch.
code: race_results <- tribble(   ~runner_name,      ~race_email,                       ~finish_time_minutes,   "Jordan Blake",    "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   47.2,   "Sam Okafor",      "sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com",     52.8,   "Nora Fitzgerald", "nora.fitz@fictionalmail.com",      61.5,   "Yusuf Demir",     "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",        44.9 )  fitness_app_leaderboard <- tribble(   ~app_username, ~app_email,                        ~total_distance_km,   "jblake_runs", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   412,   "samo_runs",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com",    298, # different email to race_results!   "yusufd",      "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",        520 )  club_roster <- tribble(   ~member_id, ~app_username,  ~race_email,                      ~app_email,   "M001",     "jblake_runs",  "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   "M002",     "samo_runs",    "sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com",   "M003",     NA,             "nora.fitz@fictionalmail.com",    NA,   "M004",     "yusufd",       "y.demir@fictionalmail.com",      "y.demir@fictionalmail.com" ) naive_join <- race_results %>%   left_join(fitness_app_leaderboard, by = c("race_email" = "app_email"))  naive_join %>% select(runner_name, race_email, total_distance_km) #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #>   runner_name     race_email                     total_distance_km #>   <chr>           <chr>                                      <dbl> #> 1 Jordan Blake    jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com               412 #> 2 Sam Okafor      sam.okafor@fictionalmail.com                  NA #> 3 Nora Fitzgerald nora.fitz@fictionalmail.com                   NA #> 4 Yusuf Demir     y.demir@fictionalmail.com                    520

title: Introduction to idmapper
text: idea: instead joining datasets directly , treat every identifier (email, username, member ID) node, link two nodes whenever co-occur row dataset. Two datasets never share identifier directly can still end connected component third dataset bridges - exactly Sam’s case.

title: Introduction to idmapper

what: 2. Mark identifier columns, and add each dataset to the graph
title: Introduction to idmapper
text: mark_id() tags column entity type ("person") kind identifier holds. add_to_identity_graph() reads tags updates graph. dataset can mark - link - one identifier type , exactly makes club_roster useful : contributes Sam’s emails app username member ID, linked ’re row.
code: race_results <- race_results %>%   mark_id(race_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   add_to_identity_graph()  fitness_app_leaderboard <- fitness_app_leaderboard %>%   mark_id(app_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   mark_id(app_username, graph = "person", type = "username") %>%   add_to_identity_graph()  club_roster <- club_roster %>%   mark_id(race_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   mark_id(app_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   mark_id(member_id, graph = "person", type = "member_id") %>%   mark_id(app_username, graph = "person", type = "username") %>%   add_to_identity_graph()

what: 3. Collapse the graph into master identities
title: Introduction to idmapper
text: Four runners , four master identities - expected, since every person genuine distinct individual. (two different people accidentally shared identifier - mistyped email reused two membership records, say - step ’d see wrongly merged one row, ’s worth eyeballing table rather trusting blindly new data source.)
code: master_runners <- generate_master_identity_table("person") #> Processing person graph... #> Extracting vertex data... #> Computing components... #> ID types found: email, username, member_id  #> Generated master table with 4 entities #> Preview: #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #>   person_id email     username  member_id #>   <chr>     <list>    <list>    <list>    #> 1 PERSON-1  <chr [1]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]> #> 2 PERSON-2  <chr [2]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]> #> 3 PERSON-3  <chr [1]> <chr [0]> <chr [1]> #> 4 PERSON-4  <chr [1]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]> #> Stored master table for 'person' master_runners #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #>   person_id email     username  member_id #>   <chr>     <list>    <list>    <list>    #> 1 PERSON-1  <chr [1]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]> #> 2 PERSON-2  <chr [2]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]> #> 3 PERSON-3  <chr [1]> <chr [0]> <chr [1]> #> 4 PERSON-4  <chr [1]> <chr [1]> <chr [1]>

what: 4. Attach master IDs back onto each dataset, and join on those instead
title: Introduction to idmapper
text: Now join person_UID instead email: Sam Okafor’s total_distance_km now correctly shows 298 - resolved via club roster bridge, special-casing required. Nora Fitzgerald correctly shows NA: ’s genuine race finisher ’s never used training app, matching failure - identity graph didn’t invent leaderboard record , just didn’t find one.
code: race_results2 <- race_results %>% join_master_ids() leaderboard2  <- fitness_app_leaderboard %>% join_master_ids()  race_results2 %>% select(runner_name, person_UID) #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #>   runner_name     person_UID #>   <chr>           <chr>      #> 1 Jordan Blake    PERSON-1   #> 2 Sam Okafor      PERSON-2   #> 3 Nora Fitzgerald PERSON-3   #> 4 Yusuf Demir     PERSON-4 leaderboard2 %>% select(app_username, person_UID) #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   app_username person_UID #>   <chr>        <chr>      #> 1 jblake_runs  PERSON-1   #> 2 samo_runs    PERSON-2   #> 3 yusufd       PERSON-4 combined <- race_results2 %>%   left_join(     leaderboard2 %>% select(person_UID, total_distance_km),     by = "person_UID"   )  combined %>% select(runner_name, finish_time_minutes, total_distance_km) #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #>   runner_name     finish_time_minutes total_distance_km #>   <chr>                         <dbl>             <dbl> #> 1 Jordan Blake                   47.2               412 #> 2 Sam Okafor                     52.8               298 #> 3 Nora Fitzgerald                61.5                NA #> 4 Yusuf Demir                    44.9               520

what: Restricting a new dataset to known people
title: Introduction to idmapper
text: Suppose fourth dataset arrives - say, RSVPs club social run - want keep rows people already known identity graph (opposed , say, guests tagging along aren’t club members). filter_by_existing_identities() without adding new identifiers edges graph: Talia Reyes dropped: email never appeared anywhere graph. Sam Okafor kept even though RSVP list app email rather one registered race - club_roster already linked app email rest identity.
code: social_run_rsvps <- tribble(   ~attendee_name, ~attendee_email,   "Jordan Blake", "jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com",   "Sam Okafor",   "samokafor.trains@fastmail.com", # his app email - still resolves, it's in club_roster   "Talia Reyes",  "talia.r@example.com"            # a friend tagging along, not a club member )  social_run_rsvps %>%   mark_id(attendee_email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   filter_by_existing_identities(env_name = "person") #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #>   attendee_name attendee_email                 #>   <chr>         <chr>                          #> 1 Jordan Blake  jordan.blake@fictionalmail.com #> 2 Sam Okafor    samokafor.trains@fastmail.com

title: Introduction to idmapper
text: Mark identifier columns [mark_id()], add dataset graph [add_to_identity_graph()]. [generate_master_identity_table()] , every dataset added. [join_master_ids()] attach resolved ID dataset, join datasets ID instead raw identifier. [filter_by_existing_identities()] restrict new dataset people/entities already known graph. payoff plain left_join() specifically cases like Sam’s: two records share identifier directly, transitively linked third dataset. data sources , bridges tend exist - naive pairwise join quietly misses.

Entity Resolution and Identity Graphs Across Multiple Data Sources
text: See vignette("idmapper") worked example (synthetic data) showing worth extra machinery plain left_join() - specifically, resolving two records share identifier directly linked transitively third dataset.
code: library(idmapper)  init_id_envs(c("person", "project"))  dataset_a <- dataset_a %>%   mark_id(email, graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   mark_id(uid, graph = "person", type = "uid") %>%   add_to_identity_graph()  dataset_b <- dataset_b %>%   mark_id(c(email_from_hr, email_from_email_list), graph = "person", type = "email") %>%   mark_id(staff_id, graph = "person", type = "staff_id") %>%   add_to_identity_graph()  generate_master_identity_table()  dataset_a2 <- dataset_a %>% join_master_ids() dataset_b2 <- dataset_b %>% join_master_ids() # both now carry a person_UID column; rows that share an identifier # (directly, or transitively through a third dataset) get the same UID
